opening.headline: When a failure occurs, we organize what to check first and who to notify first based on SLO, on-call, and response priority.
body: When an alert occurs, if the team debates whether to check the logs, revert the settings, or notify the responsible party, the impact continues to grow during that period. There must be a predefined order to properly utilize the first five minutes.

In this class, we sequentially examine the incident response process, including defining SLIs as numerical metrics, identifying the on-call pathway that reaches personnel, verifying the impact scope, mitigating the issue, and determining the root cause. We also review how incident response differs when dealing with cost and quality alert cases.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: SLO, On-call, and incident response procedures can be explained.
Response order can be determined based on impact scope and service objectives.
It is possible to determine whether the response procedure was sufficient.

screens.title: I don't know where to start when a failure occurs.
screens.lead: Consider what happens when order is not predefined, by reading about the incident that occurred on Friday evening.

visual.alt: This scene shows team members who have received failure alerts pointing in different directions and disagreeing.
labels: Let's look at the log first.
Shall we revert the model settings?

paragraphs: On Friday evening, an alert sounds indicating that the AI assistant's responses are significantly slower than usual and that some requests have failed. In the team chat, opinions diverge: some suggest checking the logs, others propose rolling back the model settings to yesterday's state, and others recommend first contacting the responsible personnel.

All three opinions are not entirely wrong. The issue is that there is no predefined order. If each party starts working on different tasks simultaneously, it becomes impossible to determine who made what changes, and during the troubleshooting process, the impact on users continues to grow.

This course integrates three components into a single workflow: SLOs that define what constitutes a failure in numerical terms, on-call responsibilities that specify who is notified and through which channels, and an incident response process that verifies the scope, mitigates impacts, and identifies root causes.

One preliminary conclusion is that the first five minutes of incident response are not about identifying the root cause, but rather about determining the extent of impact and preventing further spread.

callout.label: Note
callout.text: In this course, an incident refers to an event that may or may disrupt the normal operation of a service, and is the subject of applying response procedures.

screens.title: What do you do in the first 5 minutes of incident response?
screens.lead: Think about each question and try to recall your own answer. There is no need to input anything; when you select a question, the instructor's perspective will be revealed.

items.prompt: Is what we do in the first five minutes about identifying the root cause or about reducing the impact?
items.answer: First, it is important to understand and mitigate the impact. Root cause analysis is a time-consuming process, during which users continue to experience slow responses or failures. Verify how many requests and users are affected, and if there are any changes that can be rolled back or applied to mitigate the issue, take those actions first before diving into root cause analysis.

items.prompt: Who do we notify, and who is responsible and in charge?
items.answer: Alerts must operate on a team-based rotation system, not on an individual basis. It must be predefined who is on duty and who takes over when a response is not received. Once response begins, one person must acknowledge the alert and take command to prevent multiple individuals from making conflicting changes to the same resource.

items.prompt: What criteria can the team use to define what constitutes a defect?
items.answer: The perception of slowness varies from person to person. When response latency exceeds a few seconds or success rate drops below a certain percentage, there must be a numerical threshold defining it as a failure. That threshold is an SLO, and it is the first demonstration topic of this course.

screens.outro: Let us specifically address each of the three questions with concrete devices. First, the SLO.

screens.title: SLO: Define what constitutes a failure in numerical terms
screens.lead: Move the slider to change your success rate target. You can see how the allowed number of failures decreases as the target increases over a month.

stops.body: Looking at 30 days as 43,200 minutes, the allowable failure time is approximately 432 minutes, or roughly 7 hours and 12 minutes. SLO (Service Level Objective) is a quantitative commitment defining the target level of service that a service must meet. It indicates the extent to which the service deviates from this commitment, thereby measuring the severity of outages. A looser target results in looser alert thresholds and reduces operational burden, but it also allows for longer periods of user inconvenience.

Based on the same March 30th benchmark, the allowable downtime is approximately 43 minutes. A prolonged outage lasting several days or even a few days exceeds the monthly target by only one occurrence. Once this level is reached, when an outage occurs, personnel must verify it within a few minutes, requiring that alerting pathways and on-duty shift systems be fully established. As the target increases, the associated costs for response systems also rise.

The allowable failure time is reduced to approximately 4 minutes and 20 seconds. During the time it takes a user to see a notification and open the logs, a full month's allowance could be consumed. Achieving such goals is difficult without mechanisms like automatic scaling or instant rollback. When setting these goals, higher values are not necessarily better—instead, they should be balanced against the level of support required by users and the response capabilities that the team can realistically handle.

In AI services, objectives can extend beyond availability to include response latency, answer quality, and cost. For example, upper bounds can be set for response latency, lower bounds for evaluation scores, and upper bounds for daily token usage. Having defined objectives enables the establishment of alert thresholds, allowing differentiation between outages and normal variations when alerts are triggered. Furthermore, the degree by which objectives are exceeded serves as the basis for determining impact scope and urgency. Even when both cases—slight overage in latency and half of the requests failing—trigger the same alert, the invocation method and urgency level must differ.

screens.outro: The criteria have been established; now I'll examine the pathway by which the alert reaches a person.

screens.title: Who: Who is calling via which path?
screens.lead: When you select the image number marker, you can view descriptions of each step from the notification reaching the person.

visual.alt: The monitor alert flows through a page, passing through the Team, routing rules, escalation policies, and shift roster, ultimately reaching the assigned responder.
labels: If no response, proceed to next target

markers.label: Notification occurred
markers.title: The monitor sends a notification.
markers.body: Alerts start in places like Monitor, Incidents, and Security Signals. If you mention an oncall Team in a Monitor message, a Page is sent to that Team. For example, if the Team handles checkout-operations, you would mention @oncall-checkout-operations.

markers.label: Page
markers.title: Page is a single alert requiring attention.
markers.body: Page is a notification requiring attention from on-call responders. Its status changes in sequence: Triggered, Acknowledged, Resolved. In the Triggered state, the notification has been delivered but no one has yet taken ownership, and during this phase, the escalation policy continues to operate.

markers.label: Team and Routing
markers.title: The team receives the request and determines the urgency level.
markers.body: A Team is the central unit of OnCall. A Team's routing rules determine the priority level of a Page based on the event's metadata, or route it to another escalation policy. In Monitor, dynamic priority is set to low when the WARN threshold is exceeded and to high when the ALERT threshold is exceeded.

markers.label: escalation
markers.title: If no response is received, notify the next target.
markers.body: Escalation policy determines the order in which pages are sent to multiple duty shifts. If no response is received within the specified time, alerts are forwarded to additional responders. The escalation alert stops when someone acknowledges the page.

markers.label: This time's schedule
markers.title: Determine who is on duty for this shift.
markers.body: Schedule defines when team members will respond, organized as a timetable. It allows managing shifts across multiple time zones and rotating shifts, enabling seamless integration of work hours across Korea, Europe, and the United States.

markers.label: Resolved
markers.title: The page is closed upon recovery
markers.body: When the root cause is resolved, close the page as Resolved. If the on-call team mention appears in the recovery notification message, the page will automatically be resolved. However, if the mention is only present in the alert template and not in the recovery message, the page will not automatically close, so attention is required.

screens.outro: If a person is connected, then it remains to be determined in what order the connected person should move.

screens.title: Incident Response Workflow and Audit Tracking
screens.lead: Review the failure timeline one line at a time. The explanation on the right indicates the stage each phase represents and clarifies what problems arise if the order is inconsistent.

data.code:
18:02 [Notification] Response delay p95 > 8 seconds, request failure rate increasing (Page Triggered)
18:03 [Confirmation] Manager Kim Hae-nyeol has acknowledged the page and is now taking charge of the response and command.
18:05 [Impact Scope] Failure request is concentrated on 12% of the total, targeting a single model endpoint
18:08 [Softening] Rolling back the prompt change deployed at 17:40 to the previous version
18:12 [Confirmation] Delay and failure rate have returned within target range, received monitor recovery notification
18:13 [Completed] Page Resolved, Investigative Item Registered as Follow-up Action
18:13 [Record] Timestamp, responsible party, and change content are retained in the audit trail.

notes.note: When an alert occurs, one person must first acknowledge it and take command. This initiates the escalation alert and begins response actions. If multiple people act simultaneously without acknowledgment, conflicts may arise due to differing modifications of the same settings.

The scope refers to who is affected and to the extent of the impact. Here, the fact that 12% of the whole and a single endpoint is affected narrows down the mitigation direction. Skipping this step either results in unnecessary interventions or, conversely, misses the most critical areas.

Mitigation is an action taken to reduce impact before the root cause is confirmed. Rolling back recent changes is a typical example. If you attempt to first identify the root cause, the impact will continue during that period. After taking action, always verify that the metrics have returned within the target range.

Investigation into the root cause continues even after recovery. Follow-up actions are logged to maintain an audit trail of all activities during response. An audit trail is a record that enables the chronological reconstruction of activities leading up to a particular task. Relying on memory for later use can result in out-of-order sequences.

screens.outro: This sequence aligns with the direction specified in NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3. This guidance recommends integrating incident response into overall cybersecurity risk management, preparing for incidents, reducing the volume and impact of incidents, and improving the efficiency of detection, response, and recovery.

screens.title: Reason why responses to cost outliers and quality outliers differ
screens.lead: Compare the two alert types divided by tabs. Select each tab to read how the affected scope, mitigation, and callout differ.

tabs.label: more than cost
tabs.body: This is a notification that token usage has suddenly increased. The impact is not user inconvenience but cost. To assess the scope of impact, examine which team, feature, or key is experiencing an increase in calls. Mitigation begins by reducing inbound spikes or repeated calls. The individuals responsible for addressing this are the budget owner and the feature owner. Root cause analysis comes next.

tabs.label: more than quality
tabs.body: This alert indicates that the scoring value obtained from the evaluation has fallen below the target. Since this may suggest that users have provided incorrect answers, the nature of the impact differs. The scope of impact is determined by which question type and which user group has experienced a decline in quality. Mitigation begins with reviewing recent deployments or prompt changes, and the first point of contact should be the services team.

tabs.label: Decision sequence comparison
tabs.body: When comparing the two alerts side by side, it looks like this: For cost impact, the effect is financial loss, the scope of impact involves teams and features with increased calls, the first mitigation is to reduce inflow, and the person most affected is the budget owner. For quality impact, the effect is incorrect answers reaching users, the scope of impact involves question types with degraded quality, the first mitigation is to roll back recent changes, and the team most affected is the service team.

tabs.label: common ground
tabs.body: In both cases, the order is impact, mitigation, and root cause. The difference lies in the metrics used to measure impact, the mitigation actions, and the entities being alerted. This difference depends on how the SLO was defined. If cost and quality targets are set separately, then upon alert triggering, it is immediately clear which one has been breached, allowing for timely dispatch to the appropriate team with an escalation policy. Conversely, if all anomalies are bundled into a single alert, the person receiving the alert must first determine the type of incident, thereby extending the initial five-minute window. By separating warning (WARN) and severe (ALERT) thresholds and applying dynamic severity levels, the same metric can be categorized into low and high severity.

screens.outro: Now I will summarize the criteria for determining whether the response procedure itself is sufficient.

screens.title: Criterion for assessing whether the response procedure was sufficient
screens.lead: After the incident has ended, the instructor sequentially explains four questions to evaluate the response process. Click the following arrow to proceed step by step.

steps.title: Has the first call ever been made?
steps.body: Look at the time between when the alert is triggered and when the first call reaches and is acknowledged by the recipient. This time must align with the urgency defined by the SLO. For a 99.99% target as previously mentioned, even a few minutes of delay could be catastrophic, whereas for a 99% target, the same delay might be acceptable. Also verify that the routing rules and shift schedules are properly configured to match the defined urgency levels.

steps.title: Did one person take command?
steps.body: After acknowledgment, escalation must cease and one person must take command. If multiple individuals simultaneously changed the same setting, this indicates the procedure was inadequate. Verify that the record shows who took command and what tasks were assigned to other responders.

steps.title: Can the sequence of events be reconstructed?
steps.body: Audit trails must enable reconstruction in chronological order of who changed what and when. If explanations are only possible by stitching together memory and chat logs, then the records are insufficient. Verify that the timestamp of the change, the person who made the change, and the content of the change are properly captured during the process.

steps.title: Are any follow-up actions remaining after recovery?
steps.body: The resolution does not end simply because the indicators have returned to normal. The root cause analysis and measures to prevent recurrence must be registered as follow-up actions, with assigned owners and deadlines. Without follow-up actions, the same failure could reoccur in the same sequence. Only when all four of these conditions are met can the response procedure be considered sufficient.

screens.outro: Finally, I will summarize the content discussed so far.

screens.title: Key points and reflection
screens.lead: This is a screen summarizing the core of the lesson. Read the content and apply it to your own team.

paragraphs: SLO defines the baseline as a numerical value. With a defined baseline, alert thresholds can be established, allowing the impact scope and urgency to be assessed when performance exceeds the target.

On-call is the path through which Page reaches personnel via the team, routing rules, escalation policies, and duty roster. Page progresses in the order of Triggered, Acknowledged, Resolved, and escalation stops once it reaches Acknowledged status.

The response sequence is impact scope verification, mitigation, and root cause identification. While cost overruns and quality overruns follow the same sequence, the metrics used to assess impact scope and the mitigation measures, as well as the parties involved, differ.
Audit tracing enables the reconstruction of who did what and when after the fact, serving as evidence to determine whether the response procedure was adequate.

When checking response procedures, you only need to ask four questions: Was the first call appropriately aligned with the urgency level? Was a single person in charge? Can the sequence of events be reconstructed from records? Were follow-up actions left behind? These four questions serve as a checklist that can be repeatedly applied across different incidents. The results of this review become the basis for adjusting SLO thresholds, routing rules, and shift schedules for the next incident.

callout.label: order to remember
callout.text: Scope, mitigation, cause. The first five minutes are not about identifying the cause, but about verifying the impact and reducing it. This order must be followed regardless of whether the issue is cost-related or quality-related, or the severity of the outage.

checks.q: When the response delay alert sounds, what do we need to determine whether it indicates a fault, a normal variation, or how urgent the situation is?
options: Perceived based on manager's experience and past cases
Number of people who received the alert email
Numerical service objectives (SLO) and the degree by which they are exceeded
Whether the time of fault occurrence falls within business hours
checks.explain: A SLO must be defined to establish the threshold, and the extent to which a target is exceeded becomes the basis for determining impact scope and urgency.

wrong.0: Standards vary from person to person, leading to different judgments.
wrong.1: The number of recipients is independent of severity.
wrong.3: Time zones may affect call policies, but they are not a criterion for fault determination.

checks.intro: Check why SLO is needed. Results are not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes. A numerically defined target becomes a common benchmark for judgment.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The criteria are based on people's perceptions or coincidental facts. Reconsider where these judgment criteria originate.

checks.q: Let's look at the lifecycle of a page in OnCall, in sequential order.
items: Triggered: An alert is generated and delivered to the current user.
Acknowledged: Someone verified that the escalation alert has been stopped
Resolved: Page is terminated by recovery notifications
checks.explain: Page progresses in the order of Triggered → Acknowledged → Resolved. Once Acknowledged, escalation to the next target is halted and response begins.
checks.intro: Look at the state that each page is in, in sequence. The result is not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: The order is correct. The key point is that escalation has stopped after confirmation.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The order is incorrect. Please follow the flow again: alert is delivered, someone takes it over, and then it closes.

checks.q: When the quality exception alert (response evaluation value below target) sounds, what is the first mitigation action to review?
options: Rolling back recent deployments or prompt changes
First call the budget responsible party
Postponing user impact verification until the root cause is determined
Limiting inflows to reduce call surges
checks.explain: Quality issues may result in incorrect responses reaching users, so we first apply mitigation measures to recent changes. The order is impact scope → mitigation → root cause, analogous to cost issues.

wrong.1: The budget owner is the first point of contact regarding cost overruns.
wrong.2: It is more important to first determine the impact scope and mitigation measures rather than identifying the root cause.
wrong.3: Inflow restriction is the preferred mitigation in cost overrun alert.

checks.intro: From the quality exception alert, select the first action to review. Results are not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes, correct. Since the wrong answer is being provided to the user, rollback should take priority.
checks.incorrectFeedback: This action corresponds to another type of notification or reversed response. Consider the impact on users from a quality perspective.

glossary.def: A commitment that defines the numerical target level service must meet, serving as the threshold for alerts and the basis for fault determination.
This is a shift responsibility system in which personnel are responsible for receiving alerts and responding according to a predefined schedule.
An alert requiring attention from on-call responders and has Triggered, Acknowledged, and Resolved states.
Events that could disrupt normal operations or security, or pose a risk of doing so, are subject to response procedures.
This is a record that enables the reconstruction of activities in chronological order until a certain task is reached.

misconceptions.myth: When a failure occurs, you must first identify the cause.
misconceptions.fact: Root cause identification takes time, and during that period, the impact continues. First, determine the scope of impact, mitigate it, and then identify the root cause.

misconceptions.myth: Oncall means making a phone call to one person.
misconceptions.fact: Team, routing rules, escalation policies, and duty roster operate together. If no response is received, a notification is forwarded to the next recipient according to the policy.

misconceptions.myth: The record can be written by browsing through the memory after recovery is complete.
misconceptions.fact: Trace logs must be accumulated during response handling in order to be reconstructed chronologically afterward. Logs based on memory are prone to becoming disordered.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: SLOs are necessary to establish baselines for alerts and outages.
On-call is the path through which a Page reaches the on-duty team via escalation policies.
The response order is impact scope, mitigation, cause.
Audit tracing serves as the basis for post-incident reconstruction and response procedure evaluation.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for your own reflection only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: When our team receives a failure alert, what is the first thing we do, and is that action part of verifying the impact scope?
